description: We’re a two-person team combining engineering and design. One of us builds the simulation model and code, turning real NASA data, from solar storms to oxygen needs, into game mechanics that teach how a lunar outpost actually survives. The other is our designer, shaping the look and feel so kids aged 7–12 can understand and enjoy every decision they make. Our goal: a game where every choice involves a real engineering trade-off, and every number comes from real science.
summary: Lunar Outpost Trainer is a browser game that turns a junior astronaut into the commander of a 4-person Moon base for one lunar day (14 Earth days). Every day the player splits the solar panels’ power between making oxygen, piling regolith over the shelter against radiation, and doing science - while real solar storms from NASA’s DONKI archive arrive on the real dates they happened. Lose the air or exceed NASA’s 250 mSv single-event limit and the mission ends with an explanation of why, with the actual numbers. A Cadet mode teaches the basics with plain hints and a guided tutorial; an Engineer mode exposes the same base in real units (kWh, kg of water, mmHg of CO2, degrees C) with a battery, a water-to-oxygen chain, cabin air and thermal control, plus a built-in calculator showing the formulas. Crew members with perks and quirks, daily events with choices, and two hands-on repair mini-games make every mission different. It matters because it lets a 7-12-year-old feel the real trade-offs of living on the Moon - safety costs science, storms don’t wait for Houston - using data that is not invented.
details:
Play it in the browser: https://amiruktamovv.github.io/lunar-outpost-trainer/
Code (MIT): https://github.com/amiruktamovv/lunar-outpost-trainer

WHAT IT DOES. The player runs a lunar outpost through a random 14-day window of real space weather (Jan 2023 - Jun 2025) or the May 2024 “Gannon” storms. Each day: decide the energy split, end the day, read a report. Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are spotted leaving the Sun, so the game gives the warning time DONKI actually recorded; the crew must shelter and science stops. Solar energetic particle events (SEPs) arrive without warning: part of the dose is taken outside and shielding only helps once everyone is inside. Storms on consecutive days add up into one event, as NASA’s per-event limit treats them. The last three days are lunar sunset with 40% panel output.

TWO LEVELS. Cadet: three decisions a day in simple energy units, plain-language hints that predict tomorrow’s tank level, an 11-step coach-mark tutorial. Engineer: six systems in kWh - electrolysis, ice mining (water), CO2 scrubber, thermal loop, shielding, science - plus a 60 kWh battery and tanks that work as energy storage; new failure modes (CO2 poisoning, heat emergency, water-starved electrolyser) and an engineer’s calculator with six live tools (electrolysis, solar power, regolith shielding with inverse solving, cabin CO2, daily life-support budget, sunset planner).

REPLAYABILITY AND HANDS-ON LEARNING. Each mission has a seeded crew of four with perks (engineer, flight surgeon, geologist...) and quirks; ten daily events with choices; two mini-games - patch a leaking O2 line (pipe puzzle, 30 s) and re-align the antenna by signal strength. A mission code (?seed=N) reproduces storms, crew, events and puzzles so friends can compete on the same days. A “1.3 s” card lets the player ping Earth in real time and explains why the crew, not Mission Control, makes the calls.

HONESTY ABOUT NUMBERS. Every constant in the game is tagged on the in-game Sources screen: REAL (measured/official), PHYS (derived from physics: P = SetaA, electrolysis 4.97 kWh per kg O2, 1.125 kg water per kg O2, shielding f = exp(-k*d), ideal-gas CO2 partial pressure, t = d/c) or GAME (simplified for play, e.g. unshielded storm doses, tank sizes, scrubber power). The crew, events and mini-games are fiction; the physics they plug into is not.

HOW IT WAS BUILT. Plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, no framework, no server - opens from a file or GitHub Pages. engine.js holds all rules (no DOM) and is shared with Node balance simulators that played 500 real missions per strategy to tune difficulty (greedy play wins 66% of missions, front-loading the berm 97%; a half-powered scrubber loses 100%). Canvas effects, video backgrounds for four berm stages, coach-mark tutorials, headless smoke tests.

GOALS. Make space weather and life support intuitive for children through consequences rather than text; show that “real data” can be the game, not a footnote; give older players a path (Engineer mode) into the actual arithmetic flight controllers do.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI — Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (CCMC): all CMEs and SEPs in the game, Jan 2023 – Jun 2025
NASA Open APIs — DONKI CME/SEP endpoints used to download the storm catalogue
OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide — CO₂ SMACs (5.3 mmHg 7–180 d, 10 mmHg 24 h), 1.04 kg CO₂ per crew per day
OCHMO-TB-020 Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection — 250 mSv per solar particle event, 600 mSv career
NASA Human Integration Design Handbook (NASA/SP-2010-3407 Rev 1) — crew O₂ and CO₂ metabolic rates
OCHMO-TB-002 ECLSS: Human-Centered Approach — life-support context for electrolysis and scrubber modelling
projectRefs: Chang’E-4 LND: first measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface — background 1.369 mSv/day (Zhang et al., Science Advances 2020; CNSA / Kiel Univ. / DLR)
Lunar Sourcebook: A User’s Guide to the Moon — regolith bulk density (Heiken, Vaniman, French 1991; free PDF from LPI)
Google Flow / Veo — AI-generated scene pictures and background clips (labelled on screen)
FFmpeg — looping and compressing the background clips
Claude (Anthropic) — coding assistant and constant cross-checking
Project repository (MIT) — all code, the DONKI snapshot, in-game Sources screen with REAL / PHYS / GAME tags
